text: The Taliban has published a biography of Mullah Mohammed Omar insisting he is still alive and remains the group’s leader, apparently to counter rumors of his death. The 11-page document also seeks to bolster Omar’s militant credentials amid Islamic State’s rise and marks the anniversary of a 1996 pledge of allegiance to him.

Police and mourners gathered in South Carolina for the funeral of Walter Scott, the black man fatally shot in the back by a white officer after a traffic stop. Speakers said his death, captured on video, exposed racial injustice and could drive change; the officer has been charged with murder and fired.

A former TSA employee was sentenced to six months in jail and five and a half years’ probation for secretly filming a female co-worker in a TSA restroom, prosecutors said. Investigators also found he repeatedly entered the woman’s home and possessed more than 90 videos and 1,500 photos of her.

Cape Verde is trying to turn its rich musical heritage into an economic asset, using festivals and industry conferences to promote local artists and attract tourism. Officials say the creative sector remains small, but see music and culture as a low-cost way to raise the island nation’s global profile and spur growth.

Aaron Ramsey’s first-half goal gave Arsenal a 1-0 win at Burnley, keeping their Premier League title hopes alive and cutting Chelsea’s lead to four points before next week’s clash. Aston Villa beat Tottenham 1-0, while Leicester, Crystal Palace and Sunderland also featured in key relegation-zone results.

Original Twin Peaks cast members have launched a #SaveTwinPeaks campaign backing David Lynch in his salary dispute with Showtime. Lynch said he was exiting the nine-episode revival over insufficient money, while Showtime said it still hopes to bring the series back with both Lynch and co-creator Mark Frost.

Andrew Getty, grandson of oil tycoon J. Paul Getty, appears to have died of natural causes, Los Angeles police said. Investigators found no signs of foul play, though an autopsy is pending and medication was recovered from his home.

A Maryland woman accused of abandoning her quadriplegic son in a Philadelphia park cannot be extradited until she completes unspecified treatment, police said. The 21-year-old, who also has cerebral palsy, was found after more than four days in cold, wet conditions and is being treated for dehydration, malnutrition and other injuries.
A NASA astrophysicist has named an asteroid after Nobel laureate and girls’ education activist Malala Yousafzai. The asteroid, 316201 Malala, orbits the sun between Mars and Jupiter every 5.5 years.

A gastrointestinal illness has sickened 100 people aboard the Celebrity Infinity, including 95 of 2,117 passengers and five crew members, the CDC said. The cause has not yet been determined, and CDC staff are set to meet the ship in San Diego on Monday.

This week’s trending stories ranged from the surprise digital release of the full “Star Wars” saga to Mindy Kaling’s brother admitting he faked being Black to get into medical school. Other viral headlines included the death of “Dukes of Hazzard” actor James Best, Burger King offering a free wedding to a Burger-King couple, and Michelle Obama dancing at the White House Easter egg roll.

The FBI charged a Philadelphia woman, Keonna Thomas, with attempting to travel overseas to join ISIS after tracing social media posts and travel plans to Turkey and Spain. Two New York women were also arrested on terror charges, including allegations they plotted to build an explosive device in the U.S.

HBO released a teaser for season 2 of “True Detective,” set to premiere June 21 and starring Colin Farrell, Vince Vaughn, Rachel McAdams and Taylor Kitsch. The new season follows a murder investigation tangled in conspiracy and betrayal across California, after the first season became a breakout hit.

Authorities in Cambridge, Massachusetts, charged Carlos Colina, 32, after human remains were found in a duffel bag and later in an apartment building common area over the weekend. The victim was identified as Jonathan Camilien, 26; investigators said the men knew each other and are still determining whether more charges are warranted.

A Louisville high school basketball standout asked a freshman with Down syndrome to prom, sparking viral praise for the gesture. The girl’s family said the school’s Best Buddies program has helped her avoid isolation and build friendships.

NBC is launching “A.D. The Bible Continues,” a sequel to the History Channel’s ratings hit “The Bible,” following Jesus’ resurrection and the rise of early Christianity. The piece also previews several other TV premieres this week, including the final season run of “Mad Men” and Netflix’s “Marvel’s Daredevil.”

Indiana Gov. Mike Pence’s signing of a religious freedom law has sparked backlash and exposed the Republican Party’s deep divide over LGBT rights. The dispute is pushing GOP presidential hopefuls farther right on same-sex marriage and related issues ahead of the 2016 primaries.

Apple has released a new emoji set with more racial, ethnic and sexual-orientation diversity, including skin-tone options and same-sex couples. The changes drew praise and backlash, with some groups still saying they were left out.

Avril Lavigne said she was bedridden for five months after contracting Lyme disease, leaving her unable to breathe, talk or move at times. The singer, now “80 percent better,” said the illness was a wake-up call and will release a new single to support the 2015 Special Olympics.

New research from the Anne Frank House says Anne Frank and her sister Margot likely died at Bergen-Belsen at least a month earlier than previously believed, probably before early February 1945. The findings, based on archival records and survivor testimony, challenge the long-accepted March date of death and deepen the account of the sisters’ final days in the camp.

Two Troy University students, Ryan Calhoun and Delonte Martistee, have been arrested in Florida and charged with sexual battery by multiple perpetrators in the alleged gang rape of a woman in Panama City Beach. Authorities said the case came to light after police found video during another investigation, and more arrests are expected.

A stray dog in Washington state survived being hit by a car, struck on the head and buried alive before staggering to a nearby farm four days later, according to Washington State University. Now named Theia, the one-year-old dog is being treated for severe injuries, while a fundraising campaign for her care has topped $10,000.

The FBI says Malaysian bomb maker Zulkifli bin Hir, known as Marwan, was killed in a botched January raid in the southern Philippines and has been removed from its Most Wanted Terrorists list. The operation left 44 Philippine police dead, shattered a ceasefire with the Moro Islamic Liberation Front, and drew criticism that the drive to kill Marwan jeopardized the peace process.

The article argues the Iran nuclear framework gives Tehran too much: sanctions relief, preserved enrichment capacity and a path to retain major parts of its nuclear infrastructure. It says the deal lacks strong verification and would let Iran keep funding militant proxies while restrictions expire within a decade.

CNN previews the final season of “Mad Men,” predicting it will begin soon after the 1969 moon landing and play out amid the social and corporate upheaval of the era. The article expects major shakeups at Sterling Cooper, with possible exits for longtime characters, while Don Draper likely ends the series isolated and out of step with the times.

A giraffe at the Dallas Zoo, Katie, gave birth live on an Animal Planet stream after about an hour of labor watched by multiple cameras. The newborn’s sex and condition were not immediately known, but the zoo said the calf appeared to be moving and attempting to nurse.

Loretta Lynch’s confirmation as the first African-American woman nominated for attorney general has stalled for months, with no full Senate vote scheduled and criticism mounting over the delay. Supporters in North Carolina say the holdup reflects partisan politics and possibly race, while Republicans deny that and cite broader policy disputes.

Three people were killed and five wounded Thursday when armed assailants stormed the attorney general’s office in Balkh province, northern Afghanistan, officials said. Afghan security forces and the attackers were still exchanging fire as most staff and civilians were evacuated.

Bob Barker returned to “The Price Is Right” for the first time in eight years, briefly hosting the April 1 episode before handing duties back to Drew Carey. The 91-year-old former host looked in good form and led the first pricing game without missing a beat.

Blues legend B.B. King was hospitalized for dehydration related to Type II diabetes but has since improved and gone home to rest, his daughter said. The 89-year-old guitarist thanked fans and said he was leaving the hospital Tuesday.

A CNN commentary says the Boston Marathon verdict should prompt focus on radicalization, not on Islam itself, arguing that violence stems from politics, grievances and identity rather than the faith. It says Muslim communities and social media are increasingly exposing extremism as harmful and helping discredit its appeal.

CNN highlighted a roundup of notable videos, including a visit to Mike Tyson’s abandoned Ohio mansion, a look at the world’s tallest and fastest roller coaster, and an interview on allegations against Bikram yoga founder Bikram Choudhury. Other clips covered the Germanwings crash aftermath, a debate over Indiana’s religious freedom law, and a study on celebrity facial beauty.

The Pentagon says coalition forces have recaptured 25-30% of ISIS-held territory in Iraq, mainly in central and northern areas. A counterinsurgency expert said the gains are significant but ISIS is adapting with asymmetric attacks and propaganda to offset battlefield losses.

A passenger on an Air Canada flight from Toronto to Atlanta allegedly tried to choke a sleeping soccer player with a headphone cord about 30 minutes before landing. The suspect was subdued by other passengers, met by U.S. authorities on arrival and taken for medical/mental evaluation, with no federal charges yet pending.

A Hong Kong court adjourned until May a hearing on whether former banker Rurik Jutting, 29, should stand trial for the alleged murders of two Indonesian women found in his Wan Chai apartment last November. Police found one body on the floor and another in a suitcase on the balcony; forensic and DNA evidence is still being analyzed.

Tornadoes ripped across the rural Midwest on Thursday, killing at least one person in Fairdale, Illinois, and causing severe damage in Rochelle and nearby communities. Officials said early warnings likely saved lives, though dozens of homes were destroyed or heavily damaged and search teams were still assessing some areas.

Don McLean’s handwritten manuscript for “American Pie” sold for $1.2 million at Christie’s, the third-highest price ever for an American literary manuscript. McLean said he sold it to provide for his family as he nears 70.

UNRWA chief Pierre Krähenbühl will visit Syria’s besieged Yarmouk camp on Saturday to assess conditions and meet officials and displaced residents. The agency says 18,000 Palestinians and Syrian civilians, including 3,500 children, remain at risk amid armed group control, fighting and severe aid shortages.

Saudi-led airstrikes and ground fighting in Yemen have killed about 600 people in just over a week, with heavy damage in Sanaa and dozens more dead in Aden. The UN and Red Cross are urging a humanitarian ceasefire as power, water and medical access collapse, while al Qaeda expands in the east amid the chaos.

Former Australia captain and celebrated broadcaster Richie Benaud has died at 84 after a battle with skin cancer, prompting tributes from across the cricket world and beyond. Widely regarded as cricket’s “voice,” Benaud was praised for his playing record, captaincy and distinctive commentary style.

A nearly five-minute total lunar eclipse is visible across western North America this morning, with the total phase lasting just 4 minutes 43 seconds, the shortest of the century, NASA said. The eclipse began at 3:16 a.m. PDT and is visible in part across much of the U.S. and some of South America, Asia and Russia, but not Europe, Africa or the Middle East.

A federal grand jury has charged real estate heir Robert Durst with unlawful possession of a firearm, adding to his mounting legal troubles. Durst, already jailed on first-degree murder and other charges, awaits extradition to Los Angeles over the killing of confidante Susan Berman.

“Furious 7” opens as a tribute to Paul Walker, who died in 2013 during filming of the sequel. Producers used rewrites, special effects and Walker’s brothers as stand-ins to complete the movie, which co-star Vin Diesel said carries an emotional farewell to the actor.

A model on “The Price Is Right” accidentally revealed the correct answer in a car-guessing game, handing a contestant a new Hyundai Sonata. Host Drew Carey laughed as the blunder unfolded, while model Manuela Arbelaez was mortified but later said all was well. The mishap came during a week when former host Bob Barker returned to the show.

Thai Smile has unveiled an “Adventure Time”-themed Airbus A320 in Bangkok, with exterior and cabin designs featuring Jake, Finn and Princess Bubblegum. The themed plane is part of a partnership with Cartoon Network Amazone, with its inaugural flight set for April 4 from Bangkok to Phuket.

A mother duck and her ducklings caused a minor traffic disruption Tuesday after crossing a busy, rainy Washington street. Bystanders and a CNN crew helped corral the birds, stop traffic and escort them to a safer grassy area.

French investigators have collected the main evidence from the Germanwings Flight 9525 crash site in the Alps and do not expect to return, officials said. Authorities said the co-pilot deliberately drove the plane into the ground, killing all 150 aboard, and were still analyzing recovered debris, DNA samples and personal effects.

Cuba and the United States are at the Summit of the Americas as Washington and Havana move toward restoring diplomatic ties, including a possible embassy reopening and Cuba’s removal from the U.S. terrorism sponsors list. The thaw is complicated by Cuba’s close alliance with Venezuela and street clashes in Panama between government supporters and anti-Castro activists.

A CNN analysis says Jesus and his disciples likely survived on a subsistence mix of begging, hospitality and donations, despite his teachings on wealth. The article points to women including Mary Magdalene, Joanna and Susanna, and wealthy men such as Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus, as key financial supporters of Jesus’ ministry.

California regulators ordered PG&E to pay a record $1.6 billion penalty over unsafe gas pipeline operations, including the 2010 San Bruno blast that killed eight people. Most of the money will be spent on pipeline safety improvements, with officials saying the company failed to protect the public.

Lauren Hill, the Indiana teenager whose battle with inoperable brain cancer inspired millions, has died at 19. She became widely known after the NCAA moved up a Mount St. Joseph basketball game so she could play, and she later helped raise $1.4 million for pediatric cancer research.

A large fire broke out Friday morning at General Electric’s Appliance Park industrial site in Louisville, Kentucky, sending thick smoke over the area. Officials said there were no reports of injuries or anyone trapped, and the cause of the blaze was not immediately known.

Iranian Foreign Minister Mohammad Javad Zarif, praised for helping secure a nuclear breakthrough with the U.S., is a U.S.-educated diplomat with a less familiar past. The article notes his long American stay, disputed birth year, and earlier revolutionary activism, as talks with John Kerry now move toward a June 30 deadline.

A Connecticut judge denied a teen cancer patient’s bid to return home and rejected visitation, keeping her in temporary state custody while she completes chemotherapy for Hodgkin lymphoma. The 17-year-old is in remission and expected to finish treatment this month, after which officials say the neglect case and custody hold may be dropped.

New research using computer analysis says the 1728 play “Double Falsehood” was largely written by William Shakespeare, with help from John Fletcher and little evidence of Lewis Theobald’s authorship. The study, published in *Psychological Science*, could bolster claims that Shakespeare’s lost “Cardenio” survives in the play, though some scholars say the debate is not over.

French investigators said they have not seen any video from the Germanwings Flight 9525 wreckage, rejecting reports by Bild and Paris Match that a cell phone clip showed the final moments of the crash. Lufthansa separately confirmed co-pilot Andreas Lubitz had a history of severe depression, while investigators continued probing whether mental health issues played a role in the Alpine disaster that killed all 150 aboard.

A CNN opinion piece says American Samoans like veteran Emy Afalava are denied U.S. citizenship and voting rights despite being born on U.S. soil and subject to U.S. law. It argues the exclusion echoes discredited, racially tinged precedents and urges the federal courts to recognize their citizenship.

Blue Bell has temporarily shut its Broken Arrow, Oklahoma, plant and widened recalls after listeria was found in ice cream linked to the facility. The CDC warned consumers and institutions to discard affected products as it investigates possible ties to outbreaks in Kansas and Texas that have left five infected and three dead.

Al-Shabaab claimed responsibility for the Garissa University College attack in eastern Kenya, where many were killed and others taken hostage. The assault underscores the group’s expanding cross-border campaign and the region’s wider instability, including weak governance, exclusion and conflict.

The Pentagon says a Russian Su-27 intercepted a U.S. RC-135U reconnaissance plane over the Baltic Sea in an “unsafe and unprofessional” manner, prompting a formal complaint to Moscow. Russia said the U.S. aircraft was flying toward its border with its transponder off, which a U.S. official denied.

A hooded black angel artwork near the site of Walter Scott’s shooting has become an icon for Black Lives Matter protests in North Charleston, South Carolina. Created by local artist Phillip Hyman as a mourning piece, it has since been carried to demonstrations and widely photographed.

North Charleston officer Michael Slager has been fired and charged with murder after cellphone video appeared to show him shooting dead unarmed black man Walter Scott as Scott ran away. The footage contradicts early police accounts that said Scott took Slager’s Taser; the state investigation is ongoing.

ISIS said it seized part of Iraq’s Baiji oil refinery after launching an overnight assault, posting images it said showed fighters inside the facility. Iraqi officials denied the claim and said government forces remain in full control of the strategic refinery, a key domestic fuel source near Tikrit.

Nashville has banned prosecutors from offering female sterilization in plea deals after a public backlash, though such bargains have reportedly been used several times in recent years. The article argues the practice may be constitutionally permissible if voluntary, but says outrage stems partly from the fact that most such deals target men.

Ebola infections have fallen to their lowest weekly level since May 2014, with the WHO reporting 30 new confirmed cases in the week of April 5. But new infections continue in Guinea, and the agency warned unknown transmission chains could still spark fresh cases even as Liberia and Sierra Leone wind down surplus treatment facilities.

The NCAA says it has no legal duty to ensure the academic quality of courses or education at member schools, in response to a lawsuit by former North Carolina athletes tied to the UNC academic fraud scandal. The stance clashes with the NCAA’s long-standing rhetoric that education is central to college sports, drawing criticism from academics and athlete advocates.

An explosion and fire at a PX chemical plant in Fujian province injured six people, local authorities said. More than 600 firefighters battled the blaze, which was later brought under control, and no toxic spill was reported.

The article argues that video of a South Carolina officer shooting Walter Scott in the back shows the power of bystander footage to expose police abuse. It says body cameras could deter misconduct, improve accountability and help address broader racial bias in policing.

The Summit of the Americas in Panama is overshadowed by tensions over Venezuela, even as a historic Obama-Castro meeting looms. Maduro is rallying regional allies and drawing support from Cuba after U.S. sanctions and accusations of intervention sparked a diplomatic row.

A nuclear submarine under repair caught fire at Russia’s Zvyozdochka shipyard in a dry dock, state media reported. Officials said the blaze started during welding work, no ammunition or nuclear fuel was aboard, and no one was injured.

Philippine authorities warned of flash floods and landslides as tropical storm Maysak, locally called Chedeng, approached the country after weakening from super typhoon status. Officials banned some sea activities and carried out precautionary evacuations, with landfall expected Sunday on Isabela province’s southeastern coast.

Deion Sanders publicly teased son Deion Sanders Jr. on Twitter after the younger Sanders said he only eats “hood doughnuts.” The former NFL star reminded him he has a trust fund, condo and clothing line, and his son appeared to take the rebuke in stride.

Guatemala faces epidemic levels of gender-based violence, driven by postwar impunity, machismo and a weak justice system, with many femicides going unpunished. Survivors like Adelma Cifuentes are finding some help through activist groups, theater projects and new legal reforms, but advocates say urgent international action is still needed.

Police in Malegaon, Maharashtra, are requiring residents to photograph and register their cattle as part of enforcement of a new state ban on beef sales and consumption. Officials say the database will help track cow slaughter cases; more than 100 owners have complied amid broader backlash from beef traders and red meat consumers.

Police in Lucknow, India, are deploying drones fitted with cameras and pepper spray to control violent protests and mob attacks. The plan has drawn mixed reactions, with critics warning it could curb free speech and reflect an overreliance on force.

Christie’s sold the 16-page handwritten lyric manuscript of Don McLean’s “American Pie” for $1.2 million to an unnamed buyer. The article hails the 1971 song as an enduring American classic and cultural touchstone.

A rare, highly planned burglary at London’s Hatton Garden vault has revived comparisons to movie-style heists, with police probing possible inside involvement. Ex-detectives say such crimes are driven by profit, not thrills, and involve meticulous scouting, trusted crews, and efforts to evade forensic detection.

7-Eleven will host its first Bring-Your-Own-Cup Slurpee Day at participating U.S. stores Saturday from 11 a.m. to 7 p.m., charging $1.49 to fill a sanitary container up to 10 inches wide. The promotion kicks off peak Slurpee season and is separate from the chain’s annual Free Slurpee Day on July 11.

A Kentucky state lawmaker and civil rights trailblazer criticized Rand Paul’s presidential launch, saying his outreach to minority voters rings hollow given his record on voting rights, civil rights and other social issues. She said Paul’s positions are outdated and disqualifying, and argued the country needs more democracy, not less.

A Lamborghini crashed into a guardrail during the Exotic Driving Experience at Walt Disney World Speedway on Sunday, killing passenger Gary Terry, 36, of Davenport, Florida, authorities said. The driver, Tavon Watson, 24, of Kissimmee, lost control and suffered minor injuries. Petty Holdings said it was deeply saddened by the fatal accident.

Aaron Hernandez’s defense has rested in the Odin Lloyd murder trial after a brief case, setting up closing arguments and jury deliberations. Prosecutors relied on circumstantial evidence including testimony from Robert Kraft, Hernandez’s fiancee and footwear and video evidence, while defense lawyers sought to undermine the links to Hernandez.

China has formally detained five women’s rights activists, including Wu Rongrong, over plans to protest sexual harassment on International Women’s Day. Rights groups say the crackdown — including raids, brief detentions of supporters and denial of access to lawyers and medical care — reflects a broader push to suppress independent activism.

Martin O'Malley said Hillary Clinton's status as Democratic frontrunner is not “inevitable,” arguing history shows front-runners can fall. The former Maryland governor, considering a presidential run, said Democrats need a competitive primary even as Clinton prepares to launch her campaign Sunday.

Odin Lloyd’s family delivered emotional victim-impact statements in a Massachusetts courtroom after Aaron Hernandez was convicted of first-degree murder and sentenced to life in prison. Lloyd’s mother said she forgives those involved in his killing, while relatives remembered him as a devoted, hardworking family man and gifted athlete.

Ted Cruz is leaning hard on evangelical support in Iowa, using overtly religious appeals and social conservative themes to court the state’s influential Christian right. His strategy also aims to unite evangelicals with tea party and libertarian voters as he seeks an early boost in the GOP race.

Marvel and its rivals unveiled a string of new superhero images and cast reveals, ending fan speculation over the Vision, Daredevil, Angel and The Thing. The flurry of announcements underscored how the superhero franchise boom shows no sign of slowing.

Italy’s coast guard rescued 978 migrants in the Mediterranean off Libya, as arrivals to Europe continue to surge. The IOM says more than 10,000 migrants reached Italy in the first three months of 2015, while at least 480 have died crossing the sea this year.

French-language global broadcaster TV5Monde regained control of one of its 11 channels and its Facebook page Thursday after a cyberattack disrupted broadcasts, websites and social media. The network said it had been “hacked by an Islamist group,” with ISIS-style logos appearing online, but no one claimed responsibility.

David Lynch says he will no longer direct Showtime’s revival of “Twin Peaks,” citing insufficient funding to make the show as he wanted. Showtime said it was saddened by the decision and still hoped to bring back the cult series with Lynch and co-creator Mark Frost.

Massachusetts juries began deliberating in the trials of Dzhokhar Tsarnaev and Aaron Hernandez, both facing serious prison terms or the death penalty if convicted. Elsewhere, Rand Paul launched his presidential bid, Chicago held a closely watched mayoral runoff, and Ferguson voted under the shadow of last year’s unrest.

Tornado sirens sounded Wednesday night in Kansas as storms produced reports of twisters, including one near Goddard west of Wichita, though the storm missed the city. The weather also brought possible tornado damage, flooding and large hail to parts of Missouri, with more storms forecast Thursday across the Midwest and surrounding regions.

Jodi Arias was sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of release for the 2008 murder of her ex-boyfriend, Travis Alexander. The judge imposed the maximum penalty after two juries deadlocked on whether she should receive the death penalty.

The EPA says preliminary tests found methyl bromide in a villa at a U.S. Virgin Islands resort where a Delaware family of four fell ill and was hospitalized. Authorities are investigating whether a fumigation at the property caused the exposure and whether regulations were violated; the Justice Department has also opened a criminal probe.

A Columbia Journalism School review found Rolling Stone’s UVA gang-rape story was a major journalistic failure, prompting an apology from the magazine. The article says UVA cannot sue for defamation, while Phi Kappa Psi members may face legal hurdles because defamation claims by groups are difficult unless a small, identifiable group can show direct harm.

FBI agents shot and wounded armed robbery suspect Kevone Charleston after a confrontation outside a CVS in Forsyth County, Georgia, on Saturday. Two agents were injured in a crash during the pursuit, but were treated and released. Charleston is suspected in 32 commercial robberies dating to November 2013.

An Alaska Airlines flight from Seattle to Los Angeles returned shortly after takeoff Monday after the pilot heard banging from the cargo hold, where a ramp agent had apparently fallen asleep. The plane landed safely after a 14-minute flight; the worker was taken to hospital as a precaution and later discharged, while Alaska Airlines said it is investigating.

A judge ruled that Craig Hicks, charged in the fatal shootings of three Muslim college students in Chapel Hill, North Carolina, is eligible for the death penalty. Hicks was indicted on three first-degree murder counts after turning himself in, as investigators continue to examine whether the killings were a hate crime.

Amnesty International says Afghan authorities are doing too little to protect women’s rights activists, who face attacks from Taliban fighters, warlords and officials. The report comes after the killing of Farkhunda sparked rare female-led protests, highlighting both the deadly risks and growing defiance of women campaigning for rights in Afghanistan.

A New York judge has allowed divorce papers to be served entirely via Facebook, highlighting courts’ growing acceptance of online notice when defendants evade traditional service. The article explains that electronic service, especially private messaging or email, can be more reliable than mail, door postings or publication.

Rev. Robert H. Schuller, founder of the Crystal Cathedral and longtime host of “Hour of Power,” has died at 88 after battling esophageal cancer, his family said. The televangelist built a massive audience with his upbeat “possibility thinking” message, but his ministry later collapsed amid family succession disputes and bankruptcy.

Four workers were killed and 45 injured in a major fire Wednesday on Pemex’s Abkatun Permanente oil platform off Mexico’s coast, the state oil company said. About 300 people were evacuated, and the blaze was extinguished by nightfall; Pemex said there was no collapse or oil spill.

Kansas has enacted the first U.S. law banning a common second-trimester abortion procedure, known as dilation and evacuation, with an exception for protecting the mother’s life or health. Supporters called it a major pro-life advance, while abortion rights groups condemned it as one of the country’s most restrictive measures and vowed legal and political fightbacks.

Chinese state TV host Bi Fujian has apologized after a video showed him cursing Mao Zedong during a dinner party, prompting public outrage and an investigation by CCTV. The clip was widely circulated online before being removed from Chinese video sites, with reactions split between calls for punishment and claims he was speaking privately.

Kentucky guard Andrew Harrison apologized after a hot mic caught him using an offensive slur about Wisconsin’s Frank Kaminsky following the Wildcats’ loss. Harrison said the remark was meant in jest, and Kaminsky said he was over it after the two spoke.

“Arrested Development” is set to return for a fifth season of 17 episodes, executive producer Brian Grazer said on a podcast. Netflix did not confirm the announcement, and it was unclear whether the full cast would be back.

CERN has restarted the Large Hadron Collider after a two-year shutdown, with the first beams circulating in the 17-mile ring following final tests. Scientists hope the $3.3 billion machine will recreate conditions moments after the Big Bang and help answer major questions about mass, gravity, dark matter and the origin of the universe.

An Iranian observation plane flew within 50 yards of an armed U.S. Navy helicopter over the Persian Gulf, prompting U.S. concern it may have been a locally ordered maneuver outside senior control. No shots were fired, and the helicopter broke off without incident as Washington considers a diplomatic protest.

Dzhokhar Tsarnaev was found guilty on all 30 counts in the Boston Marathon bombing trial after 11½ hours of jury deliberation. He now faces a penalty phase in which jurors will decide whether he should receive the death penalty.

Indian police arrested four FabIndia employees after a federal minister spotted a security camera aimed at a changing room in a Goa store. Authorities charged the staff with voyeurism and breach of privacy, and are searching for the store manager as FabIndia says it is cooperating with investigators.

Iran says it will lift its ban on women attending some men’s sports events within a year, starting with certain indoor competitions. The move follows years of international criticism over the restrictions, including pressure from FIFA.

Former Satyam chairman Ramalinga Raju and nine others were sentenced to seven years in prison over India’s biggest corporate scandal, police said. Raju was also fined $804,000 after a court convicted the group over cheating and conspiracy in the $1.6 billion fraud.

Alaska Airlines apologized after removing cancer patient Elizabeth Sedway from a Hawaii-bound flight and later letting her reboard, saying staff acted out of concern for her well-being. Sedway said she was removed because she lacked a doctor’s note, causing her to miss chemotherapy and disrupting her family’s travel plans.

Turkish singer-songwriter Kayahan Acar, one of the country’s best-loved performers, died Friday in Istanbul at age 66 after a long battle with cancer. Best known for his love songs and the 1991 album “I Made a Vow,” he also competed in the 1990 Eurovision Song Contest and remained popular for decades.

Netanyahu blasted the Iran nuclear framework as a “bad deal,” saying pressure should be increased for a better agreement rather than choosing between the pact and war. Democrats defended the deal as workable, while Republicans renewed criticism and said a future president could secure tougher terms.

A shooting at the U.S. Census Bureau headquarters in Suitland, Md., and a later shootout on Washington’s H Street were linked to an apparent domestic kidnapping, police said. One guard, one officer and the suspect were wounded; the kidnapping victim was found unharmed.

Imprisoned whistleblower Chelsea Manning has joined Twitter, dictating posts through a voice phone to be published by a communications firm. Manning, serving a 35-year sentence for leaking classified documents, said she hopes the account will be interactive despite lacking internet access in prison.

Rapper Nelly was arrested in Tennessee after a state trooper stopped his private bus and said he smelled marijuana, authorities said. Police charged him with felony drug possession and found meth, marijuana, paraphernalia, handguns and small bags on the bus.

A Delaware father is improving while his two sons remain in critical condition after all four family members were sickened in a St. John villa, with federal officials suspecting pesticide exposure. The EPA says preliminary tests found methyl bromide in the unit, and the Justice Department has opened a criminal investigation.

Online journalists and bloggers in Asia face rising repression, with governments using arrests, libel laws and censorship to silence critics in places including Singapore, Malaysia, Vietnam and China. In Bangladesh, bloggers have also been targeted by extremists, with several killed in attacks that have largely gone unpunished.

Nina Dobrev says she will leave “The Vampire Diaries” at the end of this season after six years playing Elena Gilbert. The announcement sparked fan backlash over the CW show’s planned seventh season and the fate of Elena’s relationship with Damon Salvatore.

Yarmouk camp outside Damascus, once a Palestinian refugee community, has been devastated by years of fighting in Syria, with ISIS’s recent assault intensifying bombardment, shelling and street battles. About 18,000 civilians remain trapped amid shortages of food, water and medicine as aid access stays severely limited.

NASA scientists say life elsewhere in the universe may be inevitable, with estimates of billions of Earth-like, habitable-zone planets in the Milky Way. But while simple life may be common, the odds of finding communicative intelligent civilizations are far lower, and contact would likely remain elusive for centuries or longer.

A 32-year-old Massachusetts man faces murder charges after human remains were found in a duffel bag and apartment building common area in Cambridge, authorities said. The victim was identified as 26-year-old Jonathan Camilien, who knew the suspect, Carlos Colina.

Kanye West has settled a civil lawsuit brought by photographer Daniel Ramos over a 2013 assault at Los Angeles International Airport. Ramos’s lawyer said the case was dismissed after a settlement that included an apology from West, who earlier pleaded no contest to misdemeanor battery.

The article says Obama is politically invested in an Iran nuclear deal, making the U.S. appear eager for an accord while Iran gains leverage. It argues the framework deal leaves much of Iran’s nuclear infrastructure intact, eases sanctions too soon and could embolden Tehran and unsettle the Middle East.

The video of South Carolina officer Michael Slager fatally shooting Walter Scott after a traffic stop has intensified outrage and led to murder charges, but the article says it also exposes a larger problem: the U.S. lacks comprehensive data on police killings. It argues the 1994 law requiring federal tracking has gone largely unenforced, leaving the scope of police violence and racial bias unclear.

Five Americans monitored for three weeks in Omaha after Ebola exposure in Sierra Leone have been released, Nebraska Medicine said. None developed the virus; one was briefly treated for a heart-related issue but has also been discharged.

Mark Ronson and Bruno Mars’ “Uptown Funk!” logs a 13th week at No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100, extending its record as the decade’s longest-leading hit and tying for 10th-longest run in chart history. Natalie La Rose’s debut “Somebody,” featuring Jeremih, breaks into the top 10, while Maroon 5’s “Sugar” and Ed Sheeran’s “Thinking Out Loud” remain the main challengers.

CNN notes April 8 drew “Lost” fans, but also marked “Rex Manning Day,” celebrated online as a reference to “Empire Records.” The article rounds up other film-linked dates, including April 14 (“Titanic”), April 25 (“Miss Congeniality”), October 3 (“Mean Girls”) and October 21, 2015 (“Back to the Future Part II”).

Nicole Kidman’s “Grace of Monaco” is heading straight to Lifetime, where it will premiere on Memorial Day. The Weinstein Co. opted to sell the critically panned film to the cable network after weak international performance and abandoned plans for a U.S. theatrical release.

Tokyo’s Shibuya ward has passed an ordinance allowing partnership certificates for same-sex couples, giving them limited rights such as hospital visitation and tenancy co-signing. The move, a first for Japan, is nonbinding and does not equal marriage, but supporters call it a step toward wider recognition of LGBT rights.

California’s prolonged drought is rippling beyond the state, pushing up prices for some produce and beef and forcing mandatory water cuts. Officials warn the West-wide water crisis could worsen if dry conditions continue, even as wine grape quality has held up.

The University of Michigan reversed its decision and will screen “American Sniper” for students after canceling it amid objections and a petition from more than 200 students. The school said the initial cancellation was inconsistent with its values on free expression, and will also offer “Paddington” as an alternative.

Amy Schumer, Channing Tatum and Rebel Wilson delivered the biggest laughs at the 2015 MTV Movie Awards, while performances by Fall Out Boy and Charli XCX also stood out. Misfires included Schumer’s archery gag, Shailene Woodley’s rambling speech and a few tired jokes from Dwayne Johnson and others.

A 20- to 30-foot fiberglass boat fragment, suspected tsunami debris from Japan’s 2011 disaster, has been found off Oregon and towed into Newport. Officials said the debris carried yellowtail jack fish, but biologists judged the invasive-species threat to be low. The boat remains are to be dried, inspected and sent to a landfill, while the fish will go to the Oregon Coast Aquarium.

Nigeria marked one year since Boko Haram kidnapped nearly 300 schoolgirls from Chibok, with more than 200 still missing. President-elect Muhammadu Buhari vowed to step up efforts against the militants as #BringBackOurGirls continued to trend globally.

The article explains the Christian Holy Week “Easter Triduum” of Maundy Thursday, Good Friday, Holy Saturday and Easter Sunday, framing it as a progression from suffering to resurrection. It argues the sequence mirrors recurring human experience of loss, waiting and renewal, and says Easter remains resistant to commercialization.

Kenya froze 86 bank accounts linked to suspected Al-Shabaab supporters after the Garissa University massacre that killed 147 people, and officials said the list could grow. The government also launched airstrikes on militant camps in Somalia and offered a reward for a senior Al-Shabaab leader accused of organizing the attack.

Chinese-born entrepreneur Jia Jiang turned a personal fear of rejection into a viral 100-day challenge, documenting unusual requests to strangers after quitting his six-figure job. The project led to a book, speaking gigs and a wider message that rejection should be treated as a tool for growth, not failure.

Attorney General Eric Holder ordered all Justice Department employees, including federal agents and prosecutors, not to solicit or accept commercial sex, even where prostitution is legal. The memo follows reports of DEA misconduct overseas and says violators could face suspension or dismissal.

Authorities are investigating whether the fatal shooting of Wayne Community College employee Ron Lane in Goldsboro, North Carolina, was a hate crime. Police say suspect Kenneth Morgan Stancil III, a former work-study student, shot Lane in the campus print shop before fleeing to Florida, where he was arrested on a beach.

Amnesty International says governments are increasingly using the death penalty as a response to terrorism, crime and unrest, citing mass sentencing in Xinjiang, resumed executions in Pakistan and killings in Iran, Iraq and Jordan. Global executions still fell in 2014 to 607 from 778, but death sentences rose sharply, with China’s secretive toll likely far higher than the rest of the world combined.

A Duke student admitted to hanging a noose from a tree near a student union, university officials said, and will face student conduct review. Campus and criminal investigations are ongoing as students and faculty condemned the “cowardly” racist act.

Emmy-winning actor Richard Dysart, best known as Leland McKenzie on NBC’s “L.A. Law,” has died at 86 after a long illness, his family said. The veteran character actor also appeared in “That Championship Season,” “The Hospital,” “Being There,” and “The Thing.”

CNN explains Easter’s religious meaning, its shifting date and ties to lunar cycles, Passover and the Council of Nicaea. It also notes different Easter observances in the Vatican and Jerusalem, and traces the origins of Easter eggs and the bunny to later folk traditions.

Chris Rock tweeted about being stopped by police three times in seven weeks, reigniting debate over racial profiling and traffic stops involving Black drivers. His posts drew support and criticism online, including a comment from actor Isaiah Washington urging him to “adapt” to avoid police attention.

Robert Lewis Burns Jr., the original drummer for Lynyrd Skynyrd, died Friday night in a car crash in Cartersville, Georgia, state patrol said. He was 64 and was not wearing a seatbelt; no other vehicles were involved.

A cat photo has sparked a viral social media debate over whether it is going up or down a staircase. The image spread after appearing on Imgur and 9gag, with users also joking about the stairs’ design and advertisers jumping on the trend.

The U.S. and other world powers reached a framework deal in Lausanne aimed at preventing Iran from developing a nuclear weapon. The article argues the agreement’s inspections and limits are strong, rejects GOP and Israeli criticism, and says Congress should judge it on its merits.

Rolling Stone retracted its UVA gang-rape story after a Columbia Journalism School review found major fact-checking failures, but the article’s broader claims about campus sexual assault remain under scrutiny. UVA is facing state, federal and legal investigations over how it handled assault complaints, amid criticism that the controversy could deter survivors from coming forward.

Indiana Pacers forward Chris Copeland was stabbed outside a New York nightclub early Wednesday and is in stable condition, with two other people also injured. Atlanta Hawks players Pero Antic and Thabo Sefolosha were arrested nearby on obstruction and related charges after police said they interfered at the scene, though they were not involved in the stabbing.

Twisted Sister says its 2016 tour will be its last, marking the band’s 40th anniversary with a farewell run dubbed “Forty and F*ck It.” Singer Dee Snider confirmed the split, and the band will feature drummer Mike Portnoy in place of the late A.J. Pero, with two tribute shows planned in Pero’s honor.

John Travolta dismissed HBO’s Scientology documentary “Going Clear” as negative and said he has no interest in watching it. The actor praised Scientology as “brilliant,” crediting the church with helping him cope after his son Jett’s death.

“Furious 7” opened with a record $146 million weekend and drew a strong emotional response for its tribute to Paul Walker, who died before filming was completed. Fans and critics praised the ending, which retires Walker’s character Brian with a beachside farewell and montage set to “See You Again.”

HBO’s “Game of Thrones” enters its fifth season with bigger battles and major plotlines converging, including Stannis at the Wall and possible Tyrion-Daenerys contact. The season, airing in 170 countries, moves the show beyond George R.R. Martin’s books in some arcs and toward a crescendo as it passes the halfway mark.

The article recounts several rare survival stories of people lost at sea, including fishermen and castaways who endured capsized boats, engine failures and weeks to months adrift. Survivors survived on rationed water, rainwater, raw fish and sheer resourcefulness before being rescued or, in one case, swept out by a tsunami and found at sea.

The first six “Star Wars” films are coming to digital HD with new special features, including behind-the-scenes looks at the saga’s sound design. One feature spotlights how sound designer Ben Burtt created the Geonosians’ alien noises using animal sounds.

Boston Marathon bombing survivors and victims’ families reacted with relief and grief after Dzhokhar Tsarnaev was found guilty on all 30 counts in the attack and its aftermath. Many said the verdict brought accountability and a step toward closure, though no punishment can undo the losses and trauma.

China formally charged former security chief Zhou Yongkang with bribery, abuse of power and leaking state secrets, making him the highest-ranking Communist Party official ever to face corruption charges. The case is the biggest target yet in President Xi Jinping’s anti-graft campaign and will be tried in Tianjin.

Philadelphia police say a 21-year-old quadriplegic man with cerebral palsy was found abandoned in a park for more than four days, suffering from dehydration, malnutrition and other injuries. His mother was arrested in Maryland and faces multiple charges, including kidnapping and neglect, police said.

Walmart’s opposition to Arkansas’ religious freedom bill helped force Gov. Asa Hutchinson to block the measure unless it is revised, highlighting growing corporate support for LGBT equality. The retailer’s stance, along with backlash to similar laws in Indiana, is pushing Republicans and presidential contenders to balance religious-liberty arguments against anti-discrimination concerns.

A lapsed Catholic says Pope Francis has rekindled her faith by stressing humility, openness and mercy over judgment. She cites the pope’s inclusive tone, especially on gay Catholics, and a cardinal’s assurance that the church should welcome rather than reject people.

Mary Kay Letourneau Fualaau says she and husband Vili are still happily together, nearly a decade after the former teacher served more than seven years in prison for having a sexual relationship with her 13-year-old student. The couple, now parents of two teen daughters, will discuss their marriage in an ABC "20/20" interview as she seeks to teach again and have her sex offender status lifted.

Hillary Clinton’s 2016 presidential bid has been cast as a test of U.S. gender equality, with her win or loss likely to be read as a verdict on women’s political prospects. But the article says Clinton is an unusual candidate and that partisanship, not sex, will mostly determine the outcome.

Amnesty International says governments are increasingly using terrorism and security fears to justify executions, citing Pakistan and China among the worst examples. While global executions fell 22% in 2014, death sentences rose 28% to 2,466, with mass sentencing in countries including Egypt and Nigeria driving the increase.

Japan’s defense minister told parliament that Air Self Defense Force jets have never encountered extraterrestrial UFOs, after a lawmaker asked whether the military would respond to alien threats. The exchange prompted discussion of Japan’s legal and defense response to a possible invasion from outer space.

Mark Wahlberg will star in and produce “Patriots’ Day,” a CBS Films movie about the Boston Marathon bombing and the subsequent manhunt. The film, told from former Boston Police Commissioner Ed Davis’ perspective, will use research and footage gathered by CBS News’ “60 Minutes.”

Martin O’Malley and Jim Webb, both long-shot Democratic presidential hopefuls, campaigned in Iowa with sharply different styles: O’Malley worked the room aggressively, while Webb remained more reserved and issue-focused. Both are far behind Hillary Clinton in early polls, and Webb used the trip to emphasize governance, economic justice and veterans’ issues.

Turkey says nine British passport holders, including four children, were arrested at the Syria border on suspicion of trying to cross illegally into Syria. British officials said they are seeking more information from Turkish authorities.

The Justice Department has charged FedEx with 15 counts over allegedly shipping drugs and prescription medicines for illegal online pharmacies, saying the company knew or should have known about the activity. FedEx argues it was acting as a common carrier and should not be criminally liable for packages it merely transported.

Kenyans mourned 147 victims of the Garissa University College massacre, sharing personal stories and photos online under #147notjustanumber. The attack, blamed on Al-Shabaab, killed mostly students and was Kenya’s deadliest since the 1998 U.S. Embassy bombing.

Swedish photographer Johan Bavman is documenting fathers taking advantage of the country’s generous parental leave system, which offers up to 480 days with pay and incentives for shared leave. He says the project shows the bonding, exhaustion and life changes that come with extended time at home, even as few couples split the leave equally.

Obama said he is “absolutely committed” to preserving Israel’s military edge as he defended the Iran nuclear deal amid criticism from Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. He said the agreement, which would curb Iran’s nuclear program in exchange for sanctions relief, offers a chance to keep Iran from obtaining a weapon and would include U.S. support if Israel were attacked.

Indiana’s new religious-freedom law has sparked accusations it could be used to justify discrimination against gay people, reigniting debate over U.S. and state RFRA laws. The article cites cases showing these laws have mainly protected religious minorities — including Native Americans, a Brazilian church, a Sikh IRS worker and an Orthodox Jewish inmate — while courts have also rejected some claims.

Five young Chinese feminist activists may face up to five years in prison after police recommended charges over protests and planned International Women’s Day actions. The women, detained in March over campaigns against sexual harassment and domestic violence, have drawn international criticism and calls for their release.

Selena’s family says it is developing “Selena the One,” a hologram-like digital version of the late Tejano star that will sing, dance and tour. The project, led by Acrovirt LLC, aims to extend her legacy with new music and videos and is seeking $500,000 through an Indiegogo campaign.

Michele Bachmann drew outrage after likening President Obama’s Iran policy to the Germanwings co-pilot who allegedly deliberately crashed a passenger jet. Critics called the comparison despicable and divisive as nuclear negotiations with Iran continue.

Ryan Gosling says his first film as director, "Lost River," was built around Detroit’s decaying landscape, which he says gave the movie its look and tone. The divisive film centers on dereliction, violence and urban renewal, reflecting both the city’s decline and signs of rebirth.

A 19-year-old UK man was charged Wednesday with terror offenses after being arrested on arrival in Britain from Turkey, London police said. Yahya Rashid of northwest London is accused of preparing acts of terrorism and assisting others to commit them between Nov. 1 and March 31. He was due to appear in Westminster Magistrates’ Court.

CNN says Vince Neil’s mangled rendition of the U.S. national anthem at a Las Vegas Arena Football League game joined a long history of infamous celebrity performances. The article contrasts Neil’s effort with famous highs and lows from Whitney Houston, Roseanne Barr, Jimi Hendrix and Michael Bolton.

A French chalk quarry near Naours, France, has revealed an underground city covered with nearly 2,000 World War I-era soldier inscriptions, many found only recently by photographer Jeff Gusky. The carvings include names of Australians, Britons and Americans sheltering there near the Somme front, offering a rare personal record of troops who often died soon after signing their names.

The Palestinian Authority formally joined the International Criminal Court as its 123rd member, giving the court jurisdiction over alleged crimes in Palestinian territories since June 13, 2014. Israel and the United States opposed the move, while Palestinians and rights groups said it could advance accountability and justice.

Anthony Ray Hinton walked free in Alabama after nearly 30 years on death row for murders he says he did not commit. A judge dismissed the charges after firearms evidence undermined the case, and prosecutors declined to retry him.

The article argues that Americans increasingly view Tax Day as a happy occasion because most filers get refunds, tax prep is easier, and “happy endings” shape memory of the process. It says this masks deeper flaws in the U.S. tax system, which is biased against two-earner households and ordinary wage earners while favoring the wealthy.

Jordan Spieth stayed in control at the Masters, despite a double bogey on 17, and will enter Sunday four shots clear. Rory McIlroy, Tiger Woods, Phil Mickelson and Justin Rose all surged on Moving Day, but none could significantly cut into Spieth’s lead.

A Bronx woman has been charged with lying on a marriage license application after allegedly marrying 10 times, including while still legally wed to other men. Prosecutors say the serial marriages were part of an immigration scam; she pleaded not guilty and faces up to four years in prison if convicted.

An Indiana pizzeria became a flashpoint after its owners said they would not cater a same-sex wedding, triggering boycott calls, threats, and viral backlash. Supporters then raised more than $842,000 online to back the family-run business, while police investigated harassment and intimidation threats.

Vijay Chokalingam, brother of comedian Mindy Kaling, says he posed as African-American on medical school applications to boost his chances of admission and is now planning a book about it. The essay argues his stunt does not prove affirmative action gives minorities an unfair edge, citing ongoing discrimination and the need to address severe underrepresentation in medicine.

Antarctica may have set a record high of 63.5 degrees Fahrenheit at Argentina’s Esperanza Base on March 24, according to Weather Underground. The World Meteorological Organization is assembling a panel to verify the reading and determine whether it is the continent’s highest temperature on record.

U.S. officials said there is no set timetable for an Iraqi-led assault to retake Mosul from Islamic State, reversing earlier expectations of a spring offensive. They said progress is being made against ISIS, but warned the Mosul operation will be complex and require time to build.

Paddy Power has deleted a tweet linking Liverpool’s “Kop” with a racist joke referencing killings of unarmed African-American men, after widespread backlash. The bookmaker said no offense was meant, but critics condemned the post and called for the author to be fired.

Philadelphia police added attempted murder to charges against Nyia Parler, accused of leaving her quadriplegic, cerebral palsy-stricken son in the woods for more than four days while she traveled to Maryland. The 41-year-old remains in treatment in Montgomery County and cannot be extradited until it is complete.

The man accused of stabbing U.S. Ambassador Mark Lippert in Seoul has been charged with attempted murder, assaulting a foreign envoy and business obstruction, a South Korean court said. Lippert was wounded in the face and arm in the March 5 attack; police said the suspect opposed joint U.S.-South Korean military drills.

Jill Duggar Dillard, first daughter from TLC’s “19 Kids and Counting” to marry, has given birth to her first child, a 9-pound, 10-ounce son named Israel David. The baby arrived more than a week late, as Dillard and husband Derick welcomed him after preparing for the wait.

Universal’s “Furious 7” is racing toward a $135 million-$138 million North American opening, with a projected $58 million-$60 million Friday haul. The final Paul Walker film also posted a $60 million international launch and could approach $300 million worldwide by Easter Sunday, making it the biggest opening of 2015 so far.

A Secret Service supervisor has been placed on administrative leave and had his security clearance suspended after a female employee accused him of sexual assault and harassment, according to The Washington Post. The allegation adds to a string of recent scandals and security lapses that have intensified scrutiny of the agency.

Hillary Clinton is set to announce her 2016 presidential bid, with Democrats seeing her as a formidable candidate thanks to her experience and toughness. But she faces challenges over authenticity, enthusiasm from the party base, gender bias and the baggage of Bill Clinton, and will need a clear agenda beyond inevitability to win support.

The Justice Department will begin negotiating with Ferguson to overhaul its police department after finding a pattern of racial discrimination and abusive fines and arrests. The city has already seen major leadership changes, but activists say real reform will depend on sustained pressure and could include broader structural changes to local government and policing.

Etihad Airways is searching New York’s JFK Airport for Felix, the pet cat of U.S. traveler Jennifer Stewart, who disappeared after arriving from Abu Dhabi on April 1. Stewart says Felix escaped after his carrier was damaged, while the airline says the loss of pets is rare and it is reviewing handling procedures.

Louis Jordan, 37, was rescued by a cargo ship after drifting at sea for 66 days off the Carolinas in a capsized sailboat with a broken mast and shoulder. He survived storms by collecting rainwater and catching fish, and authorities said there was no reason to doubt his account. Jordan, dehydrated but in surprisingly good condition, was taken to hospital after being picked up by the Houston Express.
